headline: DNA investigation leads to arrest in 1985 Newport murder case
dek: William Morton, 61, was held without bail after Rhode Island investigators charged him in the killing of Hillary Hellewell, whose death had gone unsolved for more than four decades.
body: A 41-year-old Newport murder investigation has produced an arrest after Rhode Island authorities used new DNA analysis and investigative work to identify a potential suspect. William Morton, 61, of Smithfield was arraigned Tuesday in Newport County District Court and charged with the 1985 murder of Hillary Hellewell, a 22-year-old woman from Jamestown. The Rhode Island Attorney General’s Office announced the case with Newport police and emphasized that the charge is an allegation; Morton is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. The [Attorney General’s release](https://riag.ri.gov/press-releases/former-newport-man-charged-alleged-1985-murder-following-cold-case-investigation) says Morton was held without bail and is scheduled for a status conference Oct. 20.

Court documents cited by the Attorney General’s Office say Hellewell was killed on or about May 19, 1985, in Newport. Rhode Island Current reported that her body was found early that morning on Anthony Street, near the Newport Public Library. The case went cold after the initial investigation, leaving Hellewell’s family without a criminal defendant for decades. The arrest does not resolve the case in court, but it changes the practical posture of an investigation that had remained open without a publicly identified suspect.

The investigation was reopened in 2023 by the Newport Police Department and the Attorney General’s Cold Case Unit. According to the state, investigators used new forensic DNA analysis and investigative techniques to develop Morton as a potential suspect. Rhode Island Current’s account, based on an affidavit filed in District Court, describes a process that moved from older biological evidence to family-related DNA leads and then to a sample allegedly recovered from a water bottle Morton left at a Woonsocket concert. The affidavit says the state Department of Health later found that the bottle’s DNA profile was consistent with evidence from the 1985 case. Those are allegations presented in court documents, not findings after a trial.

The forensic work illustrates why older cases can change even when the original investigation produced no arrest. Rhode Island Current reported that evidence had been tested before but did not generate a match in the national DNA database. Later testing by a private laboratory produced relatives’ partial genetic links, investigators followed those leads, and a sample collected during surveillance supplied another comparison. The state has not said that DNA evidence alone proves the charge; prosecutors will have to present the evidence and its chain of custody as the case moves forward.

The case also highlights the role of Rhode Island’s Cold Case Unit, which was created after Attorney General Peter Neronha sought state funding in 2023. The unit includes prosecutors, investigators and a forensic genealogist who work with local police departments on unsolved homicides and unidentified-remains cases. The [unit’s public overview](https://riag.ri.gov/coldcase) says its work includes reexamining evidence, developing witnesses and applying modern technology to old cases. The Attorney General’s Office says the unit has documented more than 150 cold cases and assisted on 13 cold-case homicide investigations since its creation.

The prosecution now turns to the courts. Morton was ordered held without bail and has a status conference set for Oct. 20, according to the state. Rhode Island Current reported that he entered no plea at the District Court arraignment, as the felony case is expected to move to Superior Court. The public record will have to establish what happened in 1985, what the DNA evidence can reliably show and whether the state can prove every element of murder beyond a reasonable doubt. Until then, the arrest is a major investigative development, not a conviction.

For Newport and Jamestown, the announcement connects a current criminal proceeding to a case that has shaped the memory of two communities for more than 40 years. The Attorney General said Hellewell’s family has asked for privacy. That request, and the presumption of innocence, are central to covering the case responsibly: the new evidence may offer a path toward an answer, but the legal process still has to test the accusation in open court.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Newport 1985 murder case leads to DNA arrest
seoDescription: Rhode Island authorities charged a Smithfield man in the 1985 Newport murder of Hillary Hellewell after a DNA-led cold-case investigation.
